clue.text: Christmas stamp bearing one of the disciples

definitions.note: a noun used attributively, as in Christmas fare, matching the adjective

indicators.note: to bear something is to carry it, so one piece is held inside the other

parts.note: a seal is a stamp impressed on wax or a document
son can mean a disciple or follower, so one of them is A SON

explanation.surface: A festive postage stamp shows the face of one of Jesus's twelve apostles.
explanation.walkthrough: Christmas and stamp suggest a Christmas seal, but they split: SEAL holds A SON. The sense of son as a disciple ('sons of the prophets') is an old one.
explanation.definitionFit: Christmas is a recurring festive period of the year, so things belonging to it are tied to a particular time of year.

clue.text: Which messenger ran down to store?

definitions.text: Which messenger ran down to store?

indicators.note: to store something is to keep it inside, so the letters sit within the words

parts.note: the letters run across the end of the first word, the whole second word and the start of the third

explanation.surface: A question about which courier was sent dashing down to the shop.
explanation.walkthrough: The whole clue does both jobs: the letters sit inside the words, and the clue also describes the trip a messenger is sent on.
explanation.definitionFit: A short trip made to deliver or collect something, such as a run to the shops, is exactly the job a courier is sent out on.

clue.text: Arrange steps Johnny Walker takes when broadcasting

indicators.note: broadcasting puts words out over the air, so we go by how they sound when spoken

parts.note: a stile is a set of steps over a fence that a country walker climbs; a johnny is a chap

explanation.surface: The whisky Johnnie Walker's striding man is told to plan the steps he takes on the airwaves.
explanation.walkthrough: Johnnie Walker is a whisky brand, but here a johnny (a chap) who walks, a rambler, crosses fences by a stile, steps built into a field boundary.
explanation.definitionFit: To style hair or a display is to arrange it in a particular designed way, so the two verbs are synonyms.

clue.text: Reporting staff appointed of late do us NHS splashes

parts.note: someone appointed recently is new in the post

indicators.note: a splash scatters things about, so the letters are thrown into a new order

parts.note: taken as written, as fodder for rearranging

explanation.surface: A complaint that recently hired staff are spending lavishly on the health service at our expense.
explanation.walkthrough: The NHS is Britain's National Health Service; here its letters are just fodder. 'Splashes' reads as spends lavishly but signals the shuffle.
explanation.definitionFit: Newshounds is an informal word for journalists, the people on a paper's payroll who chase and report stories.

clue.text: Plumber's mate just seconds from clouting him!

indicators.note: taking only the second, fourth and so on means keeping every other letter

parts.note: the second, fourth, sixth, eighth and tenth letters

explanation.surface: Someone narrowly escapes a punch from a tradesman's sidekick.
explanation.walkthrough: In Nintendo's Super Mario games the plumber Mario's brother and partner is Luigi; 'just seconds' reads as moments away but means the even letters.
explanation.definitionFit: In the video game series the hero is a plumber, and his brother and constant companion fills the role of his sidekick.

clue.text: Marseille so trendy for retirement homes on the market

indicators.note: to retire is to go back, so the letters are read in the backward direction
a home houses things, so the letters live inside the clue words

parts.note: the letters straddle the end of the city, the whole small word and the start of the adjective

explanation.surface: Trendy Marseille properties are being put up for sale for people who have retired.
explanation.walkthrough: Read the run of letters backwards; 'homes' looks like the houses for sale but is the signal that the letters are housed in the words.
explanation.definitionFit: Something put up for sale is being offered to buyers, which is what being listed on the market means.

clue.text: Some year, definitively

parts.note: THE is the definite article, the word that makes a noun definite
Y is the standard abbreviation for year

explanation.surface: Some particular year, stated with certainty.
explanation.walkthrough: The definite article is pictured as the word that speaks definitively, and it goes before the year's letter.
explanation.definitionFit: In 'some say' or 'they say' the pronoun refers to unnamed people in general, so the two words fill the same slot.

clue.text: Peach someone idolised in the family slices thus

indicators.note: something that slices goes into the middle of a thing, so one piece cuts into the other

parts.note: so means thus, in this way
the person mother looks up to is MA'S HERO

explanation.surface: A peach slicing scene: a family favourite cuts the fruit up this way.
explanation.walkthrough: Ma is mother, so her hero is someone idolised at home; that phrase cuts into the short word for thus.
explanation.definitionFit: A peach is slang for something or someone excellent, and smasheroo is a jokey informal word for a real stunner.

clue.text: Publican perhaps right to put a limit on clubs, you understand?

indicators.note: limits lie on both sides of something, so one piece bounds the other

parts.note: a lien is a legal right to hold property until a debt is paid
C is the card-suit abbreviation for clubs
'See?' asks whether you follow

explanation.surface: A landlord asks if we see that he has a right to restrict the clubs nearby.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Right' tempts R, but here it is a lien, a creditor's claim on property, which surrounds the clubs letter before the closing question.
explanation.definitionFit: A British pub landlord must hold a licence to sell alcohol, so a publican is one example of a holder of such a permit.

clue.text: Go on tour of old, old city

indicators.note: touring a place means travelling all round it, so one piece goes round the other

parts.note: to have a go is to have a try
of old means old or former, and O is the abbreviation for old

explanation.surface: An invitation to take a tour of a historic city.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Old' appears twice: the first is the single letter, the second belongs to the definition.
explanation.definitionFit: The city besieged by the Greeks in Homer's Iliad is a famous ancient settlement in what is now Turkey.

clue.text: Pottage-dealer gutted crappie for serving with a little béchamel?

indicators.note: served with means placed alongside, so these pieces go after another one

parts.note: a whit is a tiny amount
in Genesis Esau sold his birthright to Jacob for a mess of pottage

indicators.note: gutting a fish removes its insides, leaving only the outside letters

parts.note: a crappie is a North American freshwater fish

explanation.surface: A cook guts a fish and serves it with a dab of creamy sauce.
explanation.walkthrough: 'A little béchamel' looks like a phrase, but 'a little' is wordplay and béchamel alone is the definition, with a question mark for definition by example.
explanation.definitionFit: Béchamel is the classic French milk sauce thickened with roux, the best-known kind of the pale sauce family.

clue.text: Fine food product that adds style a new hotel wants exposure about

indicators.note: about means around, so the following pieces wrap round the earlier one

parts.note: A taken as written, N is the abbreviation for new
H is Hotel in the NATO phonetic alphabet
to give something an airing is to expose it
gel is a hair product used for styling

explanation.surface: A fancy food item claims to add style, while a newly opened hotel wants publicity.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Fine food product' reads as one phrase, but 'product' starts the wordplay; the hotel's need for exposure is a hint to lettering, not marketing.
explanation.definitionFit: Angel hair is the thinnest strand pasta, so it is literally a very fine foodstuff.

clue.text: Some truth in Kant's thought

definitions.note: a noun, as in 'have a think'

indicators.note: some of something is only a part, so the letters are a portion of the words

parts.note: the letters run from the end of the first word into the start of the third

explanation.surface: There is a grain of truth in the philosophy of Immanuel Kant.
explanation.walkthrough: The noun sense is needed: a spell of reflection is 'a think' in informal speech.
explanation.definitionFit: Informally 'a think' is a period of considering something, which is one meaning of a spell of reflection or consideration.

clue.text: Half-hearted coxes going around in reverse lured to the back of the boat

definitions.text: to the back of the boat

indicators.note: having only half a heart means losing one of the two central letters
to go around something is to surround it, so one piece encloses the other

parts.note: a cox steers a rowing boat, so STEERS loses one of its middle Es

indicators.note: in reverse means running backwards, so those letters are flipped

parts.note: someone lured has been drawn in

explanation.surface: Lukewarm coxes circle in reverse, tempted towards the stern.
explanation.walkthrough: A cox is the person who steers a racing eight; STEERS has two hearts, the twin Es, and loses one.
explanation.definitionFit: The stern is the rear of a vessel, and adding -wards makes a direction word meaning moving towards that rear end.

clue.text: Final day letter disturbs Ironside?

indicators.note: something that disturbs breaks into the middle of another thing, splitting it

parts.note: the final part is the end
D is the abbreviation for day
mu is a Greek letter

explanation.surface: A last-day letter upsets Ironside, the wheelchair-using TV detective.
explanation.walkthrough: Ironside suggests the TV detective, but Edmund Ironside was an English king of 1016; the question mark marks the definition by nickname.
explanation.definitionFit: King Edmund II of England was nicknamed Ironside for his valour in fighting the Danes, so the nickname stands for him.

clue.text: One to add a touch of redolence after freshening up

definitions.text: One to add a touch of redolence after freshening up

indicators.note: freshening something up gives it a new look, so the letters are rearranged

parts.note: taken as written, as fodder

indicators.note: a touch is the smallest amount, so only the first letter is taken

parts.note: the opening letter of the word

explanation.surface: Something to apply for a pleasant scent once you have washed.
explanation.walkthrough: The whole clue is both the wordplay and a description of the product, applied after a shower to add a nice smell.
explanation.definitionFit: A toiletry applied after washing to mask body odour, often perfumed, is literally something that adds a pleasant scent.

clue.text: Occasions may formally request these club players

definitions.meaning: first meaning: dinner jackets, the dress code on a formal invitation
second meaning: disc jockeys who play records at a nightclub

explanation.walkthrough: 'Formally' hints at formal dress: an invitation reading 'dress: DJs' asks for dinner jackets, the British name for tuxedos. 'Club players' suggests golfers but means disc jockeys.
explanation.definitionFit: The initials stand for both dinner jackets, worn at black-tie events, and disc jockeys, who spin records in nightclubs.

clue.text: Excitement about means to enter a mainly Muslim country

indicators.note: about can mean turned round, as in about-turn, so the letters go backwards

parts.note: the rut is the season of sexual excitement in deer
a key is the means of getting in through a door

explanation.surface: Thrilled at how to get into a predominantly Islamic nation.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Means to enter' reads as a visa requirement, but means is the object that opens a lock. On Boxing Day the answer is also the leftover bird.
explanation.definitionFit: The republic straddling Europe and Asia has an overwhelmingly Islamic population, so the description identifies it.

clue.text: It's unimportant what pusher has for her

parts.note: surface reading: what a drug dealer supplies to a woman
setter's reading: pus is matter, so the word pusher with the matter taken out leaves her

explanation.surface: A shrug at what a drug dealer has in stock for a woman.
explanation.walkthrough: Split pusher as PUS + HER: pus is matter, so remove it and what is left is her. The phrase 'it doesn't matter' is the plain definition.
explanation.definitionFit: Saying something is of no importance is the standard idiom for dismissing a concern as trivial and not worth worrying about.

clue.text: Depression infusing icon, lose interest

indicators.note: to infuse is to steep one thing into another, so one piece sits inside

parts.note: an icon or idol is someone treated as a god
a col is a dip between two mountain peaks

explanation.surface: Feeling low seeps into a famous figure, who stops caring.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Depression' reads as low mood, but it is the geographical dip, the col; the idol it sits in is a god.
explanation.definitionFit: When enthusiasm fades, a person or a trail cools off; the idiom describes losing warmth of feeling or eagerness.

clue.text: Cook roast platter, one side of which he dresses

definitions.note: a clause describing the person, standing for a noun

indicators.note: to cook figures or accounts is to fiddle them, so the letters are rearranged

parts.note: taken as written, as fodder

indicators.note: a side is an edge, so only an end letter is kept

parts.note: the right-hand end of the word

explanation.surface: A cook roasts a platter of meat and dresses one side of it.
explanation.walkthrough: The kitchen picture of dressing a platter hides a tailor; sartor is a humorous Latin word for the man who makes clothes.
explanation.definitionFit: A sartor is a tailor, the man who makes and fits clothes for his customers, which is to say clothes them.

clue.text: Colour again takes focus from key photographic feature

indicators.note: to take something in is to receive it, so one piece goes inside the other

parts.note: to dye a second time is to redye

indicators.note: a focus is a central point, so only the middle letter is kept

parts.note: the centre of a three-letter word

explanation.surface: Recolouring a picture takes the attention away from its key element.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Focus' and 'photographic' suggest camera talk, but focus is the centre letter; it lands inside the dyeing word after its first three letters.
explanation.definitionFit: Flash reflecting off the retina can turn the pupils in a photo bright red, a well-known effect in snapshots.

clue.text: Timely song America omitted from merry occasion

indicators.note: something omitted is left out, so those letters are removed

parts.note: a carousal is a drunken party
USA is the United States of America

explanation.surface: A seasonal song with no Americans at a jolly party.
explanation.walkthrough: A carousal (not carousel) is a rowdy drinking bout; drop the three letters for the States from its middle.
explanation.definitionFit: Carols are songs sung at Christmas, so they are timely at the season when this puzzle appeared.

clue.text: Present is wrapped in separate block

indicators.note: something wrapped in another thing is enclosed by it

parts.note: to sunder is to split apart
the present time is now

explanation.surface: A Christmas present is wrapped in a separate package.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Present' looks like a gift being wrapped, but it is the present moment; 'block' is a verb.
explanation.definitionFit: To bury a road under drifts is to obstruct it, and figuratively to swamp someone with work, so it can mean blocking or overwhelming.

clue.text: Sci-fi author goes cycling when hell freezes over

indicators.note: cycling goes round in a loop, so letters move from the front to the back

parts.note: Jules Verne wrote early science fiction such as Twenty Thousand Leagues Under the Sea

explanation.surface: A science-fiction writer will take up cycling only in an impossible future.
explanation.walkthrough: Move the first three letters of the author's surname to the end.
explanation.definitionFit: The idiom describes a time that will not come, since hell is supposedly hot, so it means at no time at all.

clue.text: Part of harvest from oysters, being shucked in a 28

indicators.note: to shuck is to strip off a shell, so the outer letters are removed

parts.note: taken as written
the answer to 28 across

explanation.surface: Pearl-harvesting crews shuck oysters to gather what is inside.
explanation.walkthrough: The cross-reference is replaced by its answer, then the whole phrase loses its first and last letters, as an oyster loses its shell.
explanation.definitionFit: Nacre is mother-of-pearl, the iridescent lining that oysters secrete and the material pearls are made from.

clue.text: The Taj Mahal's side area overlooking the throne room?

indicators.note: in a down answer, overlooking means placed above, so one piece comes first

parts.note: A is the abbreviation for area
loo is British slang for a toilet, jokingly called the throne

explanation.surface: A wing of the Taj Mahal looks out over a royal throne room.
explanation.walkthrough: Taj Mahal is a stock name for an Indian restaurant, whose side dish is aloo (potato); the throne is a joke name for the toilet.
explanation.definitionFit: Aloo is the Hindi word for potato, served as a side dish such as Bombay aloo in Indian restaurants.

clue.text: The game's up, missus finally caught in embrace of inamorato?

indicators.note: someone caught in an embrace is held inside another's arms

parts.note: inamorato is Italian for lover, so an Italian lover is ITAL LOVER

indicators.note: finally points at the end, so only the last letter is kept

parts.note: the closing letter of the word

explanation.surface: A wife is caught with her lover and the affair is exposed.
explanation.walkthrough: Inamorato is the Italian word for a male lover, so the setter reads it as ITAL (Italian) plus LOVER; the missus is a wife.
explanation.definitionFit: Saying a game is up means the deception has been discovered and everything is finished, which is what the phrase declares.

clue.text: Team was triumphant, we hear

definitions.meaning: first meaning: a group working together, as on a ship

definitions.note: an old past tense of the verb meaning exult, so a verb phrase
definitions.meaning: second meaning: crowed, exulted, in an old past tense still heard in 'the cock ...'

explanation.surface: Reports say the team came out on top.
explanation.walkthrough: The old past tense of crow, still heard in the Bible's 'the cock crew', is spelt like the team word; 'we hear' nods to that spoken usage.
explanation.definitionFit: A group of people working together, as on a ship, fits the first sense, and the archaic past of crow means exulted.

clue.text: Grey and German, the Weihnachtsmann is here

parts.note: GR is an abbreviation for grey
Otto is a typical German man's name

explanation.surface: An elderly German man is Father Christmas.
explanation.walkthrough: Weihnachtsmann is German for Father Christmas, whom British children visit in a department-store grotto.
explanation.definitionFit: In Britain Santa traditionally receives children in a decorated cave-like booth in a shop, so that is where he is found.

clue.text: Literary companions enjoying a cider drink

definitions.meaning: first meaning: Rosie and Laurie Lee, who share cider in Lee's memoir Cider with Rosie
second meaning: Cockney rhyming slang for tea

explanation.walkthrough: Cider with Rosie is Laurie Lee's memoir of a Cotswold childhood; the girl and the author drink cider together. In rhyming slang the name rhymes with tea.
explanation.definitionFit: The name pairs the book's girl with its author, and in Cockney slang it means a cup of tea, a common drink.
